subject: get control over the names of the figures

messages.author: 074af49060f6d28c
messages.subject: get control over the names of the figures
parts:
I would like to control the name of the figures produced with knitr. The following code:

<<Figure.1.1, dev='pdf'>>=
R PLOT CODE HERE
@

produces a figure named Figure_1_1-1.pdf

I suppose that the dots are converted to underscores automatically and for good reasons and that's alright with me.

But I'd like to get rid of the appended -1, for which I have no use.

The reason is that the name Figure_1_1.pdf refers to "Figure 1.1" in a book and the appended -1 kills the beauty of my system.

Thanks for your suggestions.

messages.author: cc1ef8c8158d6b73
messages.subject: Re: [knitr] get control over the names of the figures
parts:
My suggestion is, spend more time on what Figure 1.1 is supposed to
visualize, and refrain from looking at the auto-generated filenames :)

If you really cannot sleep at night because of the annoying -1, you
may try to rename the figure file, e.g. (not tested)

library(knitr)
local({
hook_plot = knit_hooks$get('plot')
knit_hooks$set(plot = function(x, options) {
name = sub('-1([.][a-z]{3,4})$', '\\1', x)
if (name != x) file.rename(x, name)
hook_plot(name, options)
})
})

The release notes explained why -1 is necessary:
https://github.com/yihui/knitr/releases See the second bullet in the
section Major Changes of knitr 1.7

Regards,
Yihui
--
Yihui Xie <xiey...@gmail.com>

messages.author: 9ec69ca07f36d6a1
messages.subject: Re: get control over the names of the figures
parts:
If using LaTeX, you want figure names to be symbolic in case you insert or remove a figure that would cause everything to be renumbered.  So you use the chunk label as the symbolic LaTeX label and use \ref{label} to refer to it.  You can even refer to symbolic labels in comments in R code, to state which figure the code produced.

Frank

Thanks Jeff,

yes I did see that. I tried it, but something went wrong. I must have left out something important. I moved on at the time because while I like to have figures in figure environments and tables in table environments, I didn't find any doc on how to set something like ``eval.after = 'table.cap' `` to build a table environment around tables. This may simply be down to my inability to read a manual. As I am currently making beamer presentations, I have no need for references, so I let it go.

** My original question is not about figure labels or references it's about figure names. My follow-up question is that after applying Yihui's hack only the pdf figures are named Fig.pdf, while the png figures are named Fig-1.png, which I'd like to change to Fig.png, if possible. **

On the subject of references, Jeff, below is a template I wrote while attempting to have references inside a beamer environment. Something is wrong and I gave up, but of course if it's a simple thing perhaps you'll spot it right away.

Thanks for your interest!



\documentclass{beamer}
\setbeamertemplate{navigation symbols}{}

<<setup, include=FALSE>>=
library(knitr)
# evaluate fig.cap after a chunk is evaluated
opts_knit$set(eval.after = 'fig.cap')
# smaller font size for chunks
opts_chunk$set(size = 'footnotesize', fig.path='figures/')
@

\begin{document}
\title{Simple Beamer example with \texttt{knitr}}
\date{}

\maketitle

\begin{frame}
\frametitle{Required Packages}
\begin{itemize}
\item
Install the \texttt{knitr} R package.
\item
Change Tools $>$ Options $>$ Sweave from \texttt{Sweave} to \texttt{knitr}.
\item
To show the code verbatim, add the [fragile] option at the start of the frame.
\item
if fig.cap is specified, knitr generates a figure environment around the figure.
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}[fragile] % need [fragile] option
\frametitle{Figures}
Generate data from $y = x + \epsilon$, with $\epsilon \sim N(0,1)$ and plot it:
<<Figure1, fig.cap = 'Linear Regression', fig.height=3, fig.width=6, out.width='.8\\linewidth', dev='pdf', fig.align='center'>>=
    par(mar=c(4,4,.1,.1))
    x = 1:30
    e = rnorm(30)
    y = x + e
    plot(x, y)
    abline(lm(y~x))
@
\end{frame}


\begin{frame}[fragile]
\frametitle{Code Chunks}
<<tidy=FALSE>>=
summary(lm(y~x))$coefficients
@
\begin{itemize}
\item
The slope of the linear regression is: \Sexpr{coef(lm(y~x))[2]}
\item
The linear regression is displayed in Figure~\ref{fig:Figure1}
\item
The linear regression statistics are summarized in~\ref{Table1}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


\begin{frame}[fragile]
\frametitle{Tables}
\begin{itemize}
\item
Use the \texttt{xtable} package to print nice \LaTeX\ tables:
<<Table1, echo = FALSE, results = 'asis'>>=
library(xtable)
  xtable(summary(lm(y~x))$coefficients, caption ="Regression summary")
@
\item
The linear regression statistics are summarized in~\ref{Table1}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}



\begin{frame}[fragile]
\frametitle{Tikz Device}
The tikz device is straightforward and produces figures with beautiful mathematical annotations:
<<math-expr-tikz, dev='tikz', fig.width=5, fig.height=3, out.width='.55\\linewidth', cache=TRUE, message=FALSE, echo=FALSE>>=
library(ggplot2)
qplot(1:10, 1:10) +
labs(title = sprintf('$\\mathrm{d}\\mathbf{x}_{t} = \\alpha[(\\theta - \\mathbf{x}_{t})\\mathrm{d}t + %d]\\mathrm{d}B_{t}$', 4))
@
\end{frame}

\end{document}

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Re: get control over the names of the figures
parts:
Xtable creates as-is LaTeX within the knitted output, not external
files. I would not call myself a knitr expert, but AFAIK the table
labeling has to be done by xtable, not knitr.

Semi-related... unlike the xtables package, note that the tables
package does not generate an environment, so you have to include the
label yourself in raw LaTeX when you create the table environment if
you use that package.

@@ -54,7 +54,7 @@

\item
The linear regression is displayed in Figure~\ref{fig:Figure1}
\item

-The linear regression statistics are summarized in~\ref{Table1}
+The linear regression statistics are summarized in Table~\ref{Table1}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

@@ -64,12 +64,12 @@

\begin{itemize}
\item
Use the \texttt{xtable} package to print nice \LaTeX\ tables:

-<<Table1, echo = FALSE, results = 'asis'>>=
+<<, echo = FALSE, results = 'asis'>>=
library(xtable)
- xtable(summary(lm(y~x))$coefficients, caption ="Regression summary")
+ xtable(summary(lm(y~x))$coefficients, caption ="Regression
summary",label = "Table1" )
@
\item
-The linear regression statistics are summarized in~\ref{Table1}
+The linear regression statistics are summarized in Table~\ref{Table1}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

Thanks Yihui, sorry to bother you, just ignore my reply.

The problem is when dev is set to a vector, e.g. dev=c('png','pdf'), then only the first element of the vector is processed. So if the extension 'png' comes first, the figures come out as Fig1.png and Fig1-1.pdf, and if 'pdf' comes first, the figures come out as Fig1.pdf and Fig1-1.png. If a single extension is passed at a time, the string manipulation works correctly. I think it's more about how options$dev is processed during the file naming process.

perhaps it's this function that passes only the first argument of dev inside options, so that the second argument is ignored. Perhaps an lapply or sapply ...

knit_hooks$get('plot')(x, options)
